title: Huge Study Links Screen Time to Developmental Issues
paragraphs: There has been a lot of concern among educators, parents and policymakers about the dangers of spending too much time looking at screens.
A large-scale study has now linked too much screen time among children with language development issues and lower academic achievement, as well as behavioral, emotional and social problems.
The study, published in JAMA Pediatrics, was a review of existing research that included 2.8 million children aged 18 and younger in 64 countries.
The research looked at the use of a wide range of screen devices, from smartphones to television, and many common activities like scrolling through social media, gaming and video calls.
The researchers found that spending a lot of time using screens was linked to "less favorable outcomes" across many measurements of children's developmental health.

They found that children with higher levels of screen use were more likely to experience emotional issues, as well as difficulties socializing with their peers. They were also more likely to exhibit behaviors linked with anxiety and depression.

The study also found that more exposure to screens was linked with overall lower grades at school. However, when the researchers looked at specific subjects, high screen time didn't seem to have a clear link with doing poorly in math, reading or science.

But they also said these subjects are among the least studied, so there may not be enough data to be certain of this finding. And the study did find a link between high screen time and poorer language development.

Perhaps one of the more shocking findings was that the link between screen time and negative developmental and mental health outcomes was found to be equal to — and often even stronger than — links to other widely studied factors, like poverty and parental behavior.
There is something positive to take from the results, though — screen habits are something that can be changed.
The researchers wrote that their findings may help governments and medical organizations refine their guidelines on screen use among children to mitigate the worst effects.
